grammar.title: Comparatives and superlatives
grammar.summary: Use a comparative (bigger, more expensive) + than to compare two things. Use a superlative (the biggest, the most expensive) to say that one thing is more than all the others in a group.
grammar.summaryMn: Хоёр зүйлийг харьцуулахдаа comparative (bigger, more expensive) + than хэрэглэнэ. Нэг зүйл бүлэг доторх бусад бүхнээс илүү болохыг хэлэхдээ superlative (the biggest, the most expensive) хэрэглэнэ.
structure: One syllable: cheap → cheaper → the cheapest · big → bigger → the biggest (double the last letter after one short vowel)
Two syllables ending in -y: busy → busier → the busiest · noisy → noisier → the noisiest
Two or more syllables: modern → more modern → the most modern · expensive → more expensive → the most expensive
Irregular: good → better → the best · bad → worse → the worst · far → further → the furthest
A is + comparative + than B · the + superlative + in/of … (the tallest building in the city)
Bigger or smaller difference: much / a lot / far + comparative (much bigger) · a bit / slightly + comparative (a bit cheaper)

grammar.title: too / enough / (not) as … as
grammar.summary: 'Too' means more than you want or need (too expensive). 'Enough' means as much as you need (big enough, enough space). 'As … as' says two things are the same; 'not as … as' says the first is less than the second.
grammar.summaryMn: 'Too' — хэрэгцээнээс хэтэрсэн (хэт үнэтэй). 'Enough' — хангалттай (хангалттай том, хангалттай зай). 'As … as' — хоёр зүйл адилхан; 'not as … as' — эхнийх нь хоёр дахиасаа дутуу гэсэн утгатай.
structure: too + adjective / adverb: too small · too far · It's too expensive for us.
too much + uncountable noun · too many + plural noun: too much noise · too many cars
adjective + enough: big enough · not quiet enough
enough + noun: enough space · not enough parking spaces
(not) as + adjective + as: The flat is as big as the house. · The suburbs aren't as lively as the centre.
+ to-infinitive or for someone: It's too far to walk. · The room isn't big enough for two people.

usage.use: too: more than is good or possible (a negative meaning)
usage.example: The flat is too small for a family of five.
Is the kitchen big enough for a table?

usage.use: not … enough: less than you need
usage.example: There aren't enough parks in our district.

usage.use: as … as: two things are equal
usage.example: The new shopping centre is as big as a football stadium.

usage.use: not as … as: the first is less than the second
usage.example: Our street isn't as noisy as the main road.

contrast.with: too vs very · not as … as vs comparative

pairs.a: The flat is very expensive, but we can afford it.

pairs.why: 'Very' just makes the adjective stronger. 'Too' means there is a problem: it is more than we can accept.
pairs.whyMn: 'Very' зөвхөн утгыг хүчтэй болгоно. 'Too' нь асуудал байгааг буюу хүлээн авах хэмжээнээс хэтэрснийг илэрхийлнэ.

pairs.a: My room isn't as big as yours.
pairs.b: My room is smaller than yours.
pairs.why: The two sentences mean the same. 'Not as … as' often sounds softer and more polite.

mistakes.wrong: This neighbourhood is too nice! I love it.
mistakes.right: This neighbourhood is really nice! I love it.
mistakes.why: 'Too' has a negative meaning. For a positive meaning, use 'very' or 'really'.

mistakes.wrong: My flat is not as big than yours.
mistakes.right: My flat is not as big as yours.
mistakes.why: The pattern is as … as, not as … than.
mistakes.whyMn: Загвар нь as … as байна, 'as … than' биш.

pronunciation.title: Word stress: compound nouns and long words
pronunciation.explanation: In most compound nouns (two words used as one noun), the stress is on the FIRST part: BUS stop, TRAFfic jam, SHOPping centre, CAR park. In long words, the stress is often not on the first syllable: aPARTment, conVENient, afFORDable, peDEStrian. Words ending in -tion and -ity are stressed just before the ending: polLUtion, faCILity. If the stress is in the wrong place, people may not understand you, even when all the sounds are right.
pronunciation.explanationMn: Ихэнх нийлмэл нэр үгэнд (хоёр үгээс тогтсон нэг нэр) өргөлт ЭХНИЙ хэсэгт буудаг: BUS stop, TRAFfic jam, SHOPping centre. Урт үгэнд өргөлт ихэвчлэн эхний үед биш байдаг: aPARTment, conVENient, afFORDable. -tion, -ity-ээр төгссөн үгэнд өргөлт төгсгөлийн яг өмнөх үед бууна: polLUtion, faCILity. Өргөлтийг буруу газар тавибал бүх авиа зөв байсан ч сонсогч ойлгохгүй байж болно.

items.display: BUS stop · CAR park · TRAFfic jam

items.tip: Compound nouns: stress the first word.
Stress the first syllable; 'bour' is weak: /bə/.
-ity and -tion: stress the syllable just before the ending.

objectives: Use 11 words and collocations for homes and renting

warmup.intro: Where do you live: in a flat, a house or a ger? What do you like about it?

questions.prompt: Which word means 'the area of a town where you live'?

vocabulary.definition: an area of a town or city where people live
examples: We live in a quiet neighbourhood near the river.
Is this a safe neighbourhood at night?
vocabulary.mistake: Spelling: neighbour + hood. The 'gh' is silent: /ˈneɪbəhʊd/.

vocabulary.definition: an area where people live on the edge of a city, away from the centre
examples: More and more families are moving to the suburbs.
We live in a suburb about twenty minutes from the centre.
vocabulary.note: The adjective is 'suburban': a suburban street.

vocabulary.definition: large, with a lot of space inside
examples: The living room is bright and spacious.
We need a more spacious flat now that we have a baby.
vocabulary.note: Used for rooms, homes and cars, not for people.

vocabulary.definition: too small for the people or things in it
examples: Five of us lived in a cramped two-room flat.
The office feels cramped with ten desks in it.

vocabulary.definition: cheap enough for most people to pay for
examples: It's hard to find affordable housing in the city centre.
The flats in this new building are more affordable than I expected.
vocabulary.note: 'Affordable' sounds more positive than 'cheap', which can also mean 'low quality'.

vocabulary.definition: a person who owns a house or flat and rents it to other people
examples: Our landlord lives in the flat downstairs.
I called the landlord because the heating wasn't working.
vocabulary.note: For a woman, 'landlady' is also used.

vocabulary.definition: a person who pays rent to live in a house or flat
examples: The previous tenant left the flat very clean.
Tenants must pay the rent by the fifth of each month.

vocabulary.definition: money you pay when you start renting a place, which you get back later if you don't damage anything
examples: The landlord wants a deposit of one month's rent.
We got our deposit back when we moved out.
vocabulary.mistake: A deposit is not the rent. You pay rent every month; you pay a deposit once and get it back at the end.

vocabulary.definition: with furniture already in it
examples: The flat is fully furnished, so you only need to bring your clothes.
Furnished flats are usually more expensive to rent.
vocabulary.mistake: 'Furniture' is uncountable: 'a lot of furniture' or 'a piece of furniture', not 'furnitures'.

vocabulary.definition: to start living in a new home
examples: We moved in last weekend, and the flat is still full of boxes.
When are your new neighbours moving in?
vocabulary.note: Use 'move into' + a place ('We moved into a new flat') and 'move in' with no object ('We moved in on Monday').

vocabulary.definition: a system that keeps a building warm
examples: In Ulaanbaatar, the central heating usually comes on in September.
Can you turn the heating down? It's too hot in here.
vocabulary.note: 'Central heating' heats the whole building from one system.

reading.title: From a Ger District to the Fourteenth Floor
text: Until last year, I lived with my parents in a ger district in the north of Ulaanbaatar. Our house was small, but our yard was spacious: my father grew vegetables there every summer, and my little brother played football with the neighbours' children. It was a quiet neighbourhood, and everyone knew everyone.

But life there had its problems. In winter we heated the house with a coal stove, so it was always either too hot or too cold, and the air was terrible. The nearest bus stop was a twenty-minute walk away, and my commute to the office took more than an hour.

Last September I moved into a one-bedroom flat on the fourteenth floor of a new apartment block near the city centre. I'm a tenant, so I pay rent every month. My landlord, a retired engineer, asked for a deposit of two months' rent, which was difficult, but the flat is furnished, so I didn't need to buy a bed or a sofa. The best thing is the central heating: for the first time in my life, I'm warm all winter without doing anything.

Of course, it isn't perfect. The flat is quite cramped — my kitchen is about the size of our old bathroom — and I don't know any of my neighbours yet. Flats in the centre aren't very affordable either: I spend almost half of my salary on rent and bills.

Do I miss the ger district? Sometimes. On Sundays I take the bus to my parents' house, and my mother cooks buuz while my father shows me his vegetables. My parents are thinking about moving too. Many families are leaving the ger districts for flats in the suburbs, where housing is cheaper than in the centre but still has central heating. The city is changing fast, and so are we.

vocabulary.definition: buildings, services or equipment for a particular purpose, such as sports centres, hospitals and shops
examples: Our district has good sports facilities, but there's no cinema.
The new school has excellent facilities.
vocabulary.mistake: In this meaning it is usually plural: 'The facilities are good', not 'The facility is good'.

vocabulary.definition: buses, trains and trams that everyone can use
examples: Public transport in the city is cheap but very crowded in the morning.
I don't have a car, so I use public transport.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'by public transport' or 'on public transport', not 'with public transport'.

vocabulary.definition: a long line of cars that are moving very slowly or not moving at all
examples: I was stuck in a traffic jam for an hour this morning.
Traffic jams are worst between eight and nine o'clock.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'the traffic is heavy' or 'there's a lot of traffic', not 'the traffic is many'.

vocabulary.definition: dirty air, water or land that is harmful to people and nature
examples: Air pollution is the city's biggest problem in winter.
Cars and coal stoves cause a lot of pollution.
vocabulary.mistake: 'Pollution' is uncountable: 'a lot of pollution', not 'many pollutions'.

vocabulary.definition: full of people
examples: The buses are always crowded at rush hour.
The market gets very crowded at the weekend.
vocabulary.note: 'Crowded' is about people. For a room with too little space, use 'cramped'.

vocabulary.definition: a person who is walking in the street, not driving
examples: Drivers must stop for pedestrians at the crossing.
The main square is for pedestrians only — no cars are allowed.

vocabulary.definition: easy to use or reach; suitable for your plans
examples: The flat is very convenient — the bus stop is right outside.
Is Friday convenient for you?
vocabulary.mistake: People are not 'convenient'. Say 'Is 3 p.m. convenient for you?', not 'Are you convenient at 3 p.m.?'

vocabulary.definition: full of energy, activity and people
examples: Seoul Street is one of the liveliest parts of Ulaanbaatar at night.
The centre is lively, but it's also noisy.

vocabulary.definition: quiet and calm
examples: It's much more peaceful in the countryside than in the city.
We found a peaceful spot by the river for our picnic.

speaking.prompt: Compare two places you know well — for example, your home town and the city where you live now, or two districts of Ulaanbaatar. Which is better to live in, and why?
speaking.promptMn: Сайн мэддэг хоёр газраа харьцуулаарай — жишээ нь төрсөн нутаг болон одоо амьдарч буй хот, эсвэл Улаанбаатарын хоёр дүүрэг. Аль нь амьдрахад илүү вэ, яагаад?
points: Which place is the best for you, and why
phrases: The best thing about X is…
The worst thing about Y is…
speaking.sample: I'd like to compare Ulaanbaatar with my home town, Erdenet. Ulaanbaatar is much bigger and livelier than Erdenet, and the facilities are better — there are more hospitals, universities and shopping centres. However, the traffic jams are terrible, and the air pollution in winter is much worse. Erdenet is smaller and more peaceful. Public transport isn't as good, but you don't really need it because everything is close. In my opinion, Ulaanbaatar is the best place to build a career, but Erdenet is a better place to bring up children. The worst thing about the capital is the traffic — sometimes I spend more time in my car than at home!

vocabulary.definition: in or from the area near you

listening.title: You must be the new neighbour!
listening.context: Lisa moved into a new flat yesterday. Her neighbour, Ben, knocks on her door to say hello.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: Hi there! You must be the new neighbour. I'm Ben. I live in flat twelve, just opposite you.

lines.speaker: Lisa
lines.text: Oh, hi! I'm Lisa. Nice to meet you. Sorry about all the boxes — I only moved in yesterday.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: No problem at all. So, how are you finding the flat?

lines.speaker: Lisa
lines.text: I love it. It's bigger than my old place, and it's much brighter. But I don't know the area at all yet.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: Well, it's a great neighbourhood. The supermarket is just round the corner, and there's a really good local bakery opposite the bus stop.

lines.speaker: Lisa
lines.text: That's handy. What about a gym? Is there one nearby?

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: Yes, there's a sports centre about ten minutes away. It's within walking distance, but in winter most people take the bus.

lines.speaker: Lisa
lines.text: Good to know. And is it easy to find a parking space here? I've got a car.

lines.speaker: Ben

warmup.intro: When you look for a flat, what matters most to you: the price, the size or the location?

questions.prompt: Which sentence has a NEGATIVE meaning?

vocabulary.definition: the place where something is
examples: The flat is small, but the location is perfect.
We're looking for a flat in a central location.

vocabulary.definition: what you can see from a place, especially something beautiful
examples: From our window we have a great view of the mountains.
The rooms at the back don't have much of a view.
vocabulary.mistake: A 'view' is what you see from one place. For the natural area in general, use 'scenery' or 'landscape'.

vocabulary.definition: space where you can keep things when you are not using them
examples: The flat is nice, but there isn't enough storage.
We use the space under the bed for storage.
vocabulary.mistake: 'Storage' is uncountable: 'not enough storage', not 'not enough storages'.

vocabulary.definition: full of light
examples: The living room is bright because it has two big windows.
I'd like a bright flat, even if it's a bit smaller.

vocabulary.definition: a small flat with one main room for living and sleeping
examples: I rent a studio near the university.
A studio is fine for one person, but not for a couple.
vocabulary.note: British English: studio flat. American English: studio apartment.

vocabulary.definition: the money you must pay regularly for electricity, water, heating, the internet and so on
examples: The rent is 900,000 tögrög a month, plus bills.
Are bills included in the rent?
vocabulary.note: For the money you pay in a restaurant, British English says 'the bill' (American English: 'the check').

vocabulary.definition: the negative part of a situation
examples: The only downside of the flat is the noise from the road.
Living in the centre is convenient; the downside is the price.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'the downside of living there', not 'the downside to live there'.

vocabulary.definition: a small area outside an upstairs window where you can stand or sit
examples: We keep our winter vegetables on the balcony.
The flat has a small balcony with a view of the park.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'on the balcony', not 'in the balcony'.

vocabulary.definition: good enough; of an acceptable quality
examples: It's hard to find a decent flat for under a million tögrög.
The kitchen is old, but it's a decent size.
vocabulary.note: Very common in informal speech. Don't confuse 'decent' /ˈdiːsnt/ with 'descent' /dɪˈsent/.

phrases.whenToUse: In speech and informal writing, to say a place is very near. In formal writing, use 'very close to'.
phrases.example: The flat is a stone's throw from the park.

phrases.meaning: used to introduce a good point
phrases.whenToUse: When you compare good and bad points, in speech or writing.
phrases.example: On the plus side, the rent includes bills.

phrases.meaning: used to introduce a problem or the most important point
phrases.whenToUse: In conversation and informal messages, just before you explain a problem. Avoid it in formal writing.
phrases.example: I really like the flat. The thing is, it's too far from my office.

phrases.phrase: It's a bit of a trek.
phrases.meaning: It's a long, tiring walk or journey.
phrases.whenToUse: In speech and informal messages about distances.
phrases.example: The nearest supermarket is a bit of a trek, especially in winter.

phrases.whenToUse: Describing a location in a positive way, for example in adverts, emails and reviews.
phrases.example: The hotel is right in the heart of the old town.

phrases.mn: Чи байсан бол яах байсан бэ?
phrases.whenToUse: At the end of a message when you want a friend's opinion.
phrases.example: Both flats have good and bad points. What would you do?

writing.prompt: You are looking for a new flat and you have seen two. Write an email to an English-speaking friend. Describe both flats, compare them and ask for advice.
writing.promptMn: Та шинэ байр хайж байгаа бөгөөд хоёр байр үзжээ. Англиар ярьдаг найздаа имэйл бичээрэй: хоёр байраа тайлбарлаж, харьцуулаад, зөвлөгөө асуугаарай.
points: Describe the first flat (location, size, price, one downside)
Describe the second flat and compare it with the first (comparatives, not as … as)
Explain the problem (too … / not … enough) and ask for advice
writing.sample:
Hi Jess,

I've been flat-hunting all week, and I've found two decent flats. I can't decide, so I need your advice!

The first one is a studio right in the heart of the city. The location is perfect — it's a stone's throw from my office — but it's quite dark, and there isn't enough storage for all my things.

The second one is bigger and brighter, with a lovely balcony. On the plus side, the rent includes bills, so it's cheaper than the studio. The thing is, it's in the suburbs, and the bus takes forty minutes. It isn't as convenient as the first one.

What would you do?

Love,
Oyuna

reading.title: Small Space, Big Life
text: When people visit Khulan's flat for the first time, they usually say the same thing: 'Is this all?' The 27-year-old designer lives in a studio of just 22 square metres in the centre of Ulaanbaatar. Her kitchen, bedroom and living room are all in one room, and the bathroom is smaller than most people's wardrobes.

So why did she choose it? 'Location, location, location,' she laughs. 'I can walk to work in ten minutes. Most of my friends live in bigger flats in the suburbs, but they spend two hours a day in traffic. I spend that time sleeping, reading or going to the gym.'

Living in a small space has taught Khulan to be organised. Her bed folds up into the wall during the day, and there is storage everywhere: under the sofa, above the door and even under the window seat. 'The secret is not to buy too many things,' she says. 'If I buy a new jumper, an old one goes to charity.'

Of course, there are downsides. The flat isn't big enough for guests to stay overnight, and cooking a big family dinner is impossible. 'My mum wants to come for Tsagaan Sar,' Khulan says, 'but my kitchen isn't as big as her dining table!' She would also love a dog, but the studio is too small.
Does she plan to move? 'One day, when I have a family, I'll need something more spacious. But for now, this is enough for me. It's the cheapest, simplest and happiest home I've ever had.'

writing.sample: I live in Bayanzurkh, a large residential area in the east of Ulaanbaatar. It's a lively neighbourhood with plenty of facilities: there are two big supermarkets, several schools, a hospital and a sports centre. Public transport is convenient, and most buses to the centre take about twenty minutes. The area is cheaper than the city centre, so it's popular with students and young families. It's also greener — there are a few small parks where people walk their dogs in the evening. The only downside is the traffic. The main road is very crowded in the morning, and the air isn't as clean as it is in the countryside. Overall, though, it's a friendly and practical place to live.

speaking.prompt: Is it better to live in a big city or in a small town or the countryside? Give your opinion, with reasons and examples.
speaking.promptMn: Том хотод амьдрах нь дээр үү, эсвэл жижиг хот, хөдөө амьдрах нь дээр үү? Шалтгаан, жишээтэйгээр санал бодлоо хэлээрэй.
speaking.sample: In my view, it's better to live in a big city, at least when you're young. Firstly, there are more jobs, and the facilities are much better — the best hospitals and universities are in the city. Secondly, city life is livelier: there are always concerts, restaurants and new people to meet. Of course, the downside is that cities are noisier and more crowded, and the pollution in winter can be terrible. The countryside is much more peaceful, but it isn't as convenient, and you need a car for everything. So for now I'd choose the city, but maybe I'll move to the countryside when I retire.
